1. Market Overview & Long-Term Price Trend

2. Volatility Analysis & Regime Detection

Volatility was classified using a 90-day rolling annualized standard deviation of log-returns, divided into terciles: Low-Vol (<14% ann.), Medium-Vol, and High-Vol (>17% ann.). Crisis-period shading marks historically documented stress events.

Regime Statistics

RegimeTrading DaysMean Daily Return Daily Std DevSkewnessExcess Kurtosis
Low-Vol 2,082 0.0495% 0.7721% -0.152 1.929
Medium-Vol 2,145 0.0604% 0.9876% -0.278 1.697
High-Vol 2,082 0.0325% 1.4819% -0.491 5.519
Key finding: High-vol regimes exhibit markedly higher kurtosis (fat tails) and negative skewness — the characteristic signature of crisis periods where left-tail events are underestimated by normal-distribution models. Low-vol regimes show more symmetric returns with thinner tails. Regime transitions are not instantaneous; analysts should expect 20–60 day persistence once a regime is established.

Identified Crisis Periods

EventApproximate WindowCharacteristic
Global Financial CrisisSep 2008 – Jun 2009 Highest single-period volatility; sharp initial sell-off followed by record rally
European Debt CrisisAug 2011 – mid-2012 Coincided with gold ATH then rapid reversal; vol spike driven by EUR system uncertainty
COVID-19 ShockFeb 2020 – Jun 2020 Brief but extreme vol spike; gold sold off then rallied strongly as liquidity normalized

3. Seasonal & Calendar-Based Patterns

Monthly and day-of-week seasonality was analyzed using full-period log-return averages. Statistical significance was assessed via one-sample t-tests (H₀: mean = 0). Note that gold markets exhibit well-documented seasonal patterns linked to Indian wedding season demand, Chinese New Year, and Western jewelry purchasing cycles — though these are structurally weak relative to total return variance.

Seasonal takeaway: Statistically significant monthly effects are rare given gold's high daily noise (annualized vol ~18%). The heatmap reveals more about year-specific macro regimes than persistent calendar effects. Day-of-week effects are economically negligible across the full sample.

4. Return Distribution & Tail Risk

The daily log-return distribution was profiled for skewness, kurtosis, and tail behavior. Value-at-Risk (VaR) is reported at the 95th and 99th percentile loss levels using the empirical (historical simulation) method — no distributional assumptions imposed.

Jarque-Bera test: The null hypothesis of normality is rejected at all conventional significance levels (p ≪0.001). Excess kurtosis of 7.02 indicates fat tails — extreme events occur roughly 3.3× more frequently than a normal model predicts. This has material consequences for VaR and position-sizing models that assume Gaussian returns.

5. Momentum Dynamics & Liquidity Behavior

Momentum is assessed via the 50-day / 200-day MA crossover (Golden/Death Cross) system and the 20-day Rate of Change (ROC-20). Volume analysis is restricted to post-2003 data due to unreliable zero-volume records in the 2000–2003 period (documented in source_brief.md).

MA Crossover Signal Summary

SignalCount (full period)Interpretation
🆕 Golden Cross (50MA > 200MA) 16 Bullish trend transition; historically aligned with extended up-phases
🔴 Death Cross (50MA < 200MA) 16 Bearish trend transition; led into 2013–2015 correction and minor pullbacks
Volume-price relationship: Average daily volume rose materially from ~500 contracts/day (2004–2006) to peak levels during the 2008–2012 crisis and bull-market period. Volume contractions during the 2013–2015 correction are consistent with capitulation dynamics. Post-2020, volume normalization alongside rising prices suggests broad institutional participation rather than speculative excess alone.

6. Key Takeaways & Forward-Looking Considerations

  • Structural bull market: Gold has delivered 12.38% CAGR over 25 years with a Sharpe-like ratio of 0.700 — competitive with major equity indices on a risk-adjusted basis when accounting for crisis diversification benefits.
  • Volatility regime awareness is essential: Portfolio sizing and stop-loss levels should be calibrated to the current regime. High-vol regimes (Ann. Vol >17%) warrant 30–50% position reduction vs. low-vol periods. Regime persistence means signals are actionable over weeks, not days.
  • Fat tails undermine normal-model VaR: Excess kurtosis of 7.02 means standard parametric VaR (1-day 99% = -2.592% under normality) underestimates actual tail risk (empirical: -3.101%). CVaR / Expected Shortfall at 95% is -2.645% vs. VaR of -1.761% — emphasizing the severity of tail events.
  • Maximum drawdown (-44.4%): Occurred from peak (Aug 2011) to trough (Dec 2015). Investors entering at or near the 2011 peak experienced a decade-long recovery period. Position sizing must account for sustained drawdown tolerance.
  • Seasonal edges are weak: No monthly return pattern achieves high statistical significance across the full 25-year sample. Traders citing seasonal patterns should cross-reference with the current macro regime — the regime effect dwarfs the calendar effect.
  • Momentum signals have regime-conditional validity: Golden/Death Cross signals from MA crossover worked well during trending phases (2005–2011, 2018–2020) but generated false signals during choppy, sideways markets (2012–2016). Combining with volatility regime filter improves signal quality.
  • Liquidity improved structurally post-2004: Volume data before 2004 is unreliable; from 2004 onward, volumes rose and provide meaningful liquidity context. Volume surges during price advances (vs. retreats) can serve as trend-confirmation filters.
  • Current context: As of the latest data point (Mar 2026), gold is at or near all-time highs. The 90-day rolling volatility reading of 32.3% places the market in the High-Vol regime. Trend momentum (MA50 vs MA200) is Bullish (50MA above 200MA) .
For portfolio construction: Gold's low/negative correlation to equities during stress periods (as evidenced by its behavior during the 2008 GFC and 2020 COVID shock) makes it a valuable portfolio diversifier. Optimal allocation studies suggest 5–15% in a multi-asset portfolio depending on investor risk tolerance and the current volatility regime. Risk managers should use empirical VaR/CVaR rather than parametric methods given the documented fat-tail behavior.
